a: The Big Bang theory is the prevailing cosmological model for the origin of the universe. According to this theory, the universe began approximately 13.8 billion years ago as an infinitely hot and dense singularity and has been expanding ever since. In the first fraction of a second, the universe underwent a period of exponential expansion called cosmic inflation, which smoothed out irregularities and set the stage for the formation of structure. As the universe expanded and cooled, fundamental particles formed. After about 380,000 years, the universe had cooled enough for atoms to form, releasing the cosmic microwave background radiation that we can still detect today. Over hundreds of millions of years, gravity caused matter to clump together, forming the first stars and galaxies. The universe continues to expand, and observations of distant supernovae revealed that this expansion is accelerating, driven by a mysterious force called dark energy. The Big Bang is supported by multiple lines of evidence: the observed expansion of the universe (Hubble's law), the cosmic microwave background radiation, the relative abundances of light elements (hydrogen, helium, and lithium), and the large-scale structure of galaxies.

Stars are massive, luminous spheres of plasma held together by gravity, powered by nuclear fusion in their cores. Stars form in giant molecular clouds of gas and dust. When a region of the cloud becomes dense enough, gravity causes it to collapse, forming a protostar. As the protostar contracts, its core temperature rises until it reaches about 10 million degrees Celsius, at which point hydrogen fusion ignites. The star then enters the main sequence phase, where it fuses hydrogen into helium in its core. This is where most stars spend the majority of their lives. Our Sun is a main sequence star. The mass of a star determines its life cycle. Low-mass stars (like the Sun) eventually exhaust their hydrogen, expand into red giants, shed their outer layers as planetary nebulae, and leave behind white dwarfs. High-mass stars undergo more complex fusion processes, creating heavier elements up to iron, and end their lives in spectacular supernova explosions. These supernovae scatter heavy elements across space, seeding future generations of stars and planets. The remnants of massive stars become neutron stars or black holes.

A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. There are three main types of black holes. Stellar-mass black holes form when massive stars (at least 20-25 times the mass of our Sun) collapse at the end of their lives. Their masses range from a few to several dozen solar masses. Supermassive black holes contain millions to billions of solar masses and exist at the centers of most galaxies, including Sagittarius A* at the center of the Milky Way. Intermediate-mass black holes, with masses between stellar and supermassive, are the least understood and may form through the merger of smaller black holes or the collapse of massive star clusters. The boundary of a black hole is called the event horizon, the point of no return. At the center of a black hole lies the singularity, a point of infinite density where our current understanding of physics breaks down. Black holes can be detected through their gravitational effects on nearby matter and by the radiation emitted by material falling into them (accretion disks). In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope captured the first direct image of a black hole, at the center of galaxy M87.

Our solar system consists of the Sun, eight planets, five officially recognized dwarf planets, hundreds of moons, and countless asteroids, comets, and other small bodies. It formed about 4.6 billion years ago from the gravitational collapse of a molecular cloud. The Sun contains 99.86% of the solar system's mass. The four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are terrestrial, composed primarily of rock and metal. The four outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are gas and ice giants. Jupiter is the largest planet, with a mass more than twice that of all other planets combined. Saturn is famous for its spectacular ring system. Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt, containing millions of rocky objects. Beyond Neptune is the Kuiper Belt, home to Pluto and other dwarf planets, and further out still is the Oort Cloud, a spherical shell of icy bodies that is the source of long-period comets.

Dark matter and dark energy are two of the most mysterious components of our universe. Dark matter is an invisible form of matter that does not emit, absorb, or reflect light, making it detectable only through its gravitational effects. Evidence for dark matter comes from observations of galaxy rotation curves (stars at the edges of galaxies move faster than expected based on visible matter), gravitational lensing (light from distant galaxies is bent more than visible matter can explain), and the cosmic microwave background. Dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe's mass-energy content. It is likely composed of as-yet-undiscovered particles, such as WIMPs (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles) or axions. Dark energy is an even more mysterious force that is causing the expansion of the universe to accelerate. Discovered in 1998 through observations of distant supernovae, dark energy makes up about 68% of the universe. It is thought to be a property of space itself, possibly related to the cosmological constant in Einstein's equations of general relativity. Ordinary matter (everything we can see) makes up only about 5% of the universe.
